q1737: Madhushravani is a festival of newly married women in the Mithila region of Bihar, held in the month of Sawan (July–August).
q1738: Raigad Fort in Maharashtra was Shivaji's capital; he was crowned there in 1674.
Shivaji: born at Shivneri, crowned at Raigad.
q1739: The Jogi Sarangi is a bowed string instrument, so it is a chordophone; string instruments are chordophones.
Chordophone = strings; aerophone = air; membranophone = skin; idiophone = body itself vibrates.
q1740: The Khazana Building Museum near Golconda, Hyderabad (Telangana), displays sculptures from the Kakatiya and Chalukya periods.
Golconda fort is in Hyderabad too.
q1741: Tippani is a Gujarati folk dance, so pair I is correct. Domkach belongs to Jharkhand and Bihar (not Assam) and Khoria to Haryana (not Rajasthan), so pairs II and III are wrong.
q1742: An indirect tax is paid by one person but its burden passes to another, e.g. customs duty, GST and excise. Income, wealth and estate taxes are direct.
Direct = on income or wealth; indirect = on goods and services.
q1743: The Repo Rate and the Liquidity Adjustment Facility are RBI monetary-policy tools. The currency–deposit ratio depends on how much cash the public holds, so it is not an RBI instrument.
RBI tools: repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, OMO, LAF, MSF.
q1744: Personal Disposable Income = Personal Income − Personal tax payments − Non-tax payments (fines, fees).
PDI is what households can spend or save.
q1745: The Consumer Price Index tracks the change in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services; the change is expressed as a percentage.
CPI (Combined) is the RBI's inflation target measure (4% ± 2%).
q1746: The National Human Rights Commission was set up on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
It is a statutory body, not a constitutional one.
q1747: Haemoglobin, the iron-containing protein that carries oxygen, is found in red blood cells.
Platelets clot blood; WBCs fight infection; plasma is the liquid part.
q1748: Molecular mass is the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule. Moles = given mass ÷ molar mass (not the reverse), and molar mass is the mass of one mole, so only statement I is right.
q1749: Pancreatic juice contains trypsin; mucus protects the stomach lining from hydrochloric acid; gastric glands are in the stomach wall. All three statements are correct.
q1750: Frequency = 1 / time period, and sound travels faster in water (about 1,480 m/s) than in oxygen (about 316 m/s). Persistence of sound from repeated reflections is reverberation, not echo, so only I and II are right.
Echo = one clear reflection; reverberation = many overlapping ones.
q1751: Igneous rocks are called primary rocks because they form first, from cooled magma, and other rocks form from them.
q1752: Limestone, mica and gypsum are all non-metallic minerals; iron ore, bauxite and copper are metallic.
Mica: Jharkhand, Andhra Pradesh; gypsum: Rajasthan.
q1753: Solar and tidal energy are both renewable because they are naturally replenished; coal, oil and gas are non-renewable.
Gulf of Khambhat and Kutch have tidal energy potential.
q1754: Annapurna (8,091 m) is in Nepal. Kanchenjunga (Sikkim) and Kamet (Uttarakhand) are in India, and India counts Nanga Parbat as part of Ladakh/PoK.
q1756: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro was a large brick tank lined with bitumen, with rooms on all sides (NCERT); it was probably used for ritual bathing.
q1757: Raziyya (Razia Sultan), daughter of Iltutmish, ruled Delhi from 1236 to 1240; she was the only woman to rule the Delhi Sultanate.
Iltutmish named her his successor over his sons.
q1758: Qutbuddin Aibak built the first storey of the Qutub Minar (about 1199); Iltutmish added three storeys and Firoz Shah Tughlaq repaired the top.
Aibak started it, Iltutmish finished it.
q1759: Guru Ghasidas founded the Satnami movement in Chhattisgarh in the early 19th century, preaching equality and rejecting caste and idol worship.
Chhattisgarh's Guru Ghasidas University is named after him.
q1760: The Tenzing Norgay National Adventure Award is India's highest award for adventure sports on land, sea and air.
Named after Tenzing Norgay, who climbed Everest with Hillary in 1953.
q1761: 'Lessons Life Taught Me Unknowingly' (2019) is the autobiography of actor Anupam Kher.
Kher also wrote 'The Best Thing About You Is You'.
q1763: DRDO is headquartered in New Delhi, not Mumbai, so statement I is wrong; its vision is to empower India with cutting-edge defence technologies.
q1768: FASTag uses Radio Frequency Identification (RFID): a tag on the windscreen is read by radio waves at the toll plaza, and the toll is deducted automatically.
NHAI runs FASTag; it became mandatory in February 2021.
q1769: The Third Schedule contains the forms of oaths and affirmations for ministers, MPs, MLAs, judges and the CAG.
1st: states and UTs; 2nd: salaries; 3rd: oaths; 4th: Rajya Sabha seats.
q1770: Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment. Article 14 is equality before law, 17 abolishes untouchability, 18 abolishes titles.
q1771: Trusts and trustees, actionable wrongs, and forests (moved there by the 42nd Amendment) are all in the Concurrent List.
42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife and justice administration to the Concurrent List.
q1772: Under Article 66 a Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha.
President: qualified for the Lok Sabha; Vice-President: for the Rajya Sabha.
q1773: The 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 21A (free and compulsory education for ages 6–14), changed Article 45 and added the 11th Fundamental Duty.
Right to Education Act followed in 2009.
q1774: India won 69 medals (15 gold, 24 silver, 30 bronze) at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta–Palembang, its best tally until 2023.
q1775: The Davis Cup is a men's tennis team event (not table tennis); the Fed Cup, now the Billie Jean King Cup, is the women's tennis team event.
q1776: Handball and artistic gymnastics are long-standing Summer Olympic sports; surfing joined at Tokyo 2020.
Tokyo 2020 also added skateboarding, sport climbing and karate.
q1780: Chad Sukra is a sowing festival of the Pnar (Jaintia) people of Meghalaya, held in April–May.
Other Meghalaya festivals: Nongkrem, Wangala, Behdienkhlam.
q1781: The Sundari is a double-reed wind instrument like a small shehnai, from Maharashtra.
Khartal: wooden clappers; santoor: struck strings; surando: bowed strings.
q1782: Fatehpur Sikri is near Agra in Uttar Pradesh. Feroz Shah Kotla, Humayun's Tomb and Safdarjung's Tomb are in Delhi.
q1783: Cheraw, the bamboo dance, belongs to Mizoram; dancers step between clapping bamboo poles.
q1784: The Kamakhya temple stands on Nilachal hill in Guwahati, Assam; it is one of the most important Shakti peeths.
The Ambubachi Mela is held there every June.
q1785: India has a mixed economy, where public and private sectors exist side by side, adopted under the Nehru-era plans.
USSR: socialist; USA: capitalist; India: mixed.
q1786: National Disposable Income = Net National Product at market prices + other current transfers from the rest of the world (NCERT Macroeconomics).
NDI measures how much the nation can spend.
q1787: NCERT Macroeconomics: a proportional income tax acts as an automatic stabiliser (tax falls as income falls), and firms are taxed on a proportional basis as a fixed share of profits.
Automatic stabilisers soften booms and slumps without new decisions.
q1788: The RBI's total liability, currency held by the public plus bank reserves with the RBI, is called the monetary base or high-powered money (M0).
M0 = high-powered money; M3 = broad money.
q1789: The Balance of Payments is a systematic record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world; its two main parts are the current account and the capital account.
q1790: The three equations of uniformly accelerated motion are v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² − u² = 2as. 'u = 1/(at²)' is not one of them.
v = u + at is the first.
q1791: In the modern periodic table atomic radius DECREASES from left to right (more nuclear charge) and INCREASES down a group (more shells), so both statements are wrong.
Across a period: smaller; down a group: bigger.
q1792: Vertebrates have a notochord (at least in the embryo), are triploblastic (three germ layers, not diploblastic) and coelomate, so I and III are correct.
q1793: Human hearing is about 20 Hz–20 kHz (not 30–30 kHz), and ultrasound is above 20 kHz (not 15 kHz), so I and IV are wrong. The pinna is the outer ear, and ultrasound does detect flaws in metal.
q1794: The natural environment includes land, water, air, plants and animals: everything not made by humans.
The human-made environment: buildings, roads, bridges.
q1795: The Pole Star (Polaris) sits almost directly above the North Pole, so it always shows the north direction.
It is found using the pointer stars of the Great Bear (Saptarishi).
q1796: The ionosphere, within the thermosphere (about 80–400 km), reflects radio waves back to earth and makes long-distance radio transmission possible.
q1797: Nanga Parbat is about 8,126 m high, the western anchor of the Himalayas and the ninth-highest mountain in the world.
q1798: Gautama Buddha was born a Kshatriya prince of the Shakya clan at Lumbini; Mahavira was also a Kshatriya.
q1799: The Battle of Buxar (1764) was won by the British over Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II; it led to the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) and the Diwani of Bengal.
q1800: Rabindranath Tagore founded the school at Santiniketan (1901), which grew into Visva-Bharati University (1921).
UNESCO listed Santiniketan as a World Heritage Site in 2023.
The Santiniketan ashram itself was set up earlier, in 1863, by his father Debendranath Tagore; Rabindranath is credited with the school and university there.
q1801: C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru formed the Swaraj Party on 1 January 1923 to contest council elections and oppose government from inside the legislatures.
Formed after Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation (Chauri Chaura, 1922).
q1802: Babur ruled 1526–1530 and Akbar 1556–1605, so both pairs are correct.
q1803: A.P.J. Abdul Kalam is called the Missile Man of India for leading the Agni and Prithvi missile programmes; he was President from 2002 to 2007.
Homi Bhabha: nuclear programme; Vikram Sarabhai: space programme.
q1804: The Raja Ram Mohan Roy Award is given by the Press Council of India on National Press Day (16 November) for outstanding contribution to journalism.
Ram Mohan Roy published 'Sambad Kaumudi' and 'Mirat-ul-Akhbar'.
q1805: 'Listening, Learning and Leading' (2019), released by Amit Shah, records Vice-President M. Venkaiah Naidu's second year in office.
q1806: The World Bank and the IMF are both headquartered in Washington, D.C., USA; both came from the Bretton Woods Conference (1944).
q1812: Article 52 says there shall be a President of India; Article 53 vests the Union's executive power in him.
q1813: Dogri and Bodo, along with Maithili and Santhali, were added to the Eighth Schedule by the 92nd Amendment (2003), which now lists 22 languages.
q1814: The 61st Amendment Act, 1988 lowered the voting age from 21 to 18 for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections (in force from 1989).
q1815: Article 54 covers the President's election (by an electoral college) and Article 58 the qualifications for election as President, so both are correct.
Article 55: manner of election; 56: term; 61: impeachment.
q1816: Ajay Thakur captained India's Kabaddi team to the 2016 World Cup; Manoj Tiwary is a cricketer, so only pair II is correct.
Anup Kumar and Pardeep Narwal are other Kabaddi stars.
q1817: England (London) hosted the 2018 FIH Women's Hockey World Cup; the Netherlands won it.
Men's Hockey World Cup 2018 was in Bhubaneswar.
q1818: The Uber Cup is the women's world team badminton championship and the Hopman Cup a mixed-team tennis event, so both pairs are correct.
Thomas Cup: men's badminton (India won in 2022).
q1821: Pongal is Tamil Nadu's four-day harvest festival in mid-January, marking the sun's movement north (Makar Sankranti).
Bhogi, Thai Pongal, Mattu Pongal, Kaanum Pongal.
q1822: Amer (Amber) Fort near Jaipur is in Rajasthan; Bellary Fort is in Karnataka, so only II is correct.
Amer is part of the UNESCO 'Hill Forts of Rajasthan'.
q1823: The dhak, a large drum, is closely linked with West Bengal's Durga Puja, so pair II is correct. The damaru is not a Gujarat instrument, so pair I is the wrong one.
q1824: Hozagiri is a folk dance of the Reang (Bru) community of Tripura, performed balancing on pitchers.
q1825: Sua is a Chhattisgarh dance, not Haryana's, so pair II is wrong; Chhau is performed in West Bengal (Purulia) and Kelika is listed among Andhra Pradesh's folk dances.
q1826: The trade balance is the value of exports minus imports of goods; a positive balance is a trade surplus and a negative one a trade deficit.
Trade balance covers goods only; the current account adds services and transfers.
q1827: The capital account records international purchases and sales of assets such as money, stocks, bonds, loans and FDI.
Current account = goods, services, transfers; capital account = assets.
q1828: The share of deposits banks keep as reserves (lending out the rest) is the reserve–deposit ratio (NCERT Macroeconomics).
The RBI's minimum requirement is set through CRR and SLR.
q1829: The Wholesale Price Index measures prices at which goods are traded in bulk; in the USA a similar index is called the Producer Price Index.
q1830: The RBI's monetary policy aims mainly at price stability while keeping growth in mind, and the repo rate is its main policy instrument.
Monetary Policy Committee: 6 members, set up 2016.
q1831: Tooth enamel starts to dissolve when the mouth's pH falls below about 5.5, from acids made by bacteria breaking down sugars.
Toothpaste is basic to neutralise the acid.
q1833: In a concave mirror, an object at infinity forms a highly diminished image at the focus; an object at the focus forms a highly enlarged image at infinity; an object at C forms a same-size image at C (not enlarged). So I and III are right.
At C → same size at C.
q1834: J.J. Thomson's 'plum pudding' model: the atom is a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it, and positive and negative charges are equal. Electrons revolving around a nucleus came later with Rutherford and Bohr.
Thomson = plum pudding; Rutherford = nucleus; Bohr = orbits.
q1835: The Tropic of Cancer lies at about 23½°N; the Tropic of Capricorn at 23½°S; the Arctic Circle at 66½°N.
The Tropic of Cancer passes through eight Indian states.
q1836: Iron ore and bauxite (aluminium ore) are both metallic minerals.
Metallic: iron, bauxite, copper, manganese; non-metallic: mica, limestone, gypsum.
q1837: Granite is an intrusive igneous rock (cooled slowly underground, large crystals); basalt is extrusive (cooled quickly at the surface).
Intrusive = inside the earth = coarse grains.
q1838: India has large iron ore deposits (Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Jharkhand); Bangladesh has almost none, so only I is correct.
Bailadila (Chhattisgarh) is a major iron ore mine.
q1839: Viceroy Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, sparking the Swadeshi movement; the partition was annulled in 1911.
1905 partition → 1911 annulment → capital moved to Delhi.
q1840: India's first successful cotton textile mill was set up in Bombay in 1854 by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar.
The first jute mill came up at Rishra, Bengal (1855).
Some books name the Bowreah mill at Fort Gloster near Calcutta (1818) as the first cotton mill; the usual answer, and DSSSB's key, is Bombay (1854).
q1841: Chandragupta Maurya and his son Bindusara were Mauryan rulers; Prithviraj Chauhan was a 12th-century Chahamana king.
q1842: After the Second Round Table Conference failed, Gandhi relaunched the Civil Disobedience Movement in January 1932; it was withdrawn in 1934.
CDM: launched 1930 (Dandi March), paused by the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931), relaunched 1932.
q1843: Magadha rose under Bimbisara and his son Ajatashatru, and Rajagriha (Rajgir) was its capital before it moved to Pataliputra.
Magadha was one of the 16 Mahajanapadas.
q1844: The International Monetary Fund is headquartered in Washington, D.C., like the World Bank.
IMF and World Bank = Bretton Woods twins (1944).
q1846: 'The Unquiet River: A Biography of the Brahmaputra' (2019) is by historian Arupjyoti Saikia.
The Brahmaputra is called the Tsangpo in Tibet and Jamuna in Bangladesh.
q1848: G.S. Lakshmi became the first woman to referee a men's ODI (2019) and the first woman on the ICC International Panel of Match Referees.
She had played first-class cricket for South Zone.
q1854: War and peace, extradition and railways are all Union List subjects (List I of the Seventh Schedule).
Union List ~100 subjects; State List ~61; Concurrent ~52.
q1855: Maharashtra has a bicameral legislature (Assembly and Council); Kerala has only a Legislative Assembly.
Six states have Legislative Councils: UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh.
q1856: Part IX (The Panchayats) was inserted by the 73rd Amendment (1992); Part IXA (Municipalities) by the 74th.
